summary_html: Family agrees to a **voluntary service plan**—counseling, substance-use treatment, parenting classes—designed to correct conditions without court compulsion. Federal law prioritizes family preservation through prevention and support services.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Harris v. Lynchburg Division of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination as to the mother but reversed as to the father, holding that undisputed evidence that a parent was never offered or provided services overcomes the statutory prima facie case and puts the agency to full proof of the § 16.1-283(C)(2) factors.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Virginia rule that the failure to offer voluntary services defeats termination even when the statutory prima facie triggers are met.
key_cases.quote: where, as here, there is undisputed evidence that a parent has not been offered or provided services, the prima facie case is overcome

key_cases.case_name: Weaver v. Roanoke Department of Human Resources
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed the termination of both parents' residual parental rights because the record contained no evidence that social agencies made the 'reasonable and appropriate efforts' that Code § 16.1-283(C)(2) requires before rights may be severed, and directed that termination statutes be read to preserve the parent-child relationship where possible.
key_cases.relevance: The Court reversed termination where the record showed no agency assistance was ever offered, which is the direct legal consequence of skipping voluntary services.
key_cases.quote: Statutes terminating the legal relationship between parent and child should be interpreted consistently with the governmental objective of preserving, when possible, the parent-child relationship.

key_cases.case_name: Richardson v. Henry County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(B)(2), holding that proof that the mother without good cause failed to respond to available and reasonable rehabilitative efforts is statutory prima facie evidence of the (B)(2) conditions, which the mother then failed to rebut.
key_cases.relevance: The extensive list of services the Department made available is what converted the case into a prima facie termination case when the mother did not respond.
key_cases.quote: Under the statute, this is prima facie evidence of the conditions set forth in subparagraph (B)(2) of the statute.

key_cases.case_name: Toombs v. Lynchburg Division of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(C)(2), holding that whether parental visitation must continue after a termination petition is filed is decided case by case with the child's best interests as the guiding principle, and that clear and convincing evidence supported the statutory factors here.
key_cases.relevance: It treats the services the Division actually offered the parents as the measure of whether the family's failure to correct conditions was 'without good cause'.
key_cases.quote: The question must be resolved, however, in light of the facts of each case, with the best interests of the child as the guiding principle.

key_cases.case_name: Kaywood v. Halifax County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that the three statutory prima facie triggers are not the only means of proving that the conditions causing the abuse cannot be corrected, and that whether correction is possible 'within a reasonable time' is judged from the context and attendant circumstances.
key_cases.relevance: The father argued the Department never offered or provided him any rehabilitative services, and the Court held that the absence of that statutory prima facie trigger does not by itself defeat a subsection (B) case.
key_cases.quote: The phrase, “within a reasonable time” is not definable by any prescribed rule. Its meaning depends upon the context and the attendant circumstances; not upon mere opinion or expectation.

key_cases.case_name: Toms v. Hanover Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that rehabilitative services are a relevant concern but not an absolute prerequisite to a subsection (B) termination and that due process imposes no constitutional duty to provide them, while distinguishing subsection (C), which turns on the parent's failure to remedy problems during a period in which services were offered.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Virginia authority separating the two statutory tracks: the offer of services is the measure under subsection (C), but is a relevant factor rather than a condition precedent under subsection (B).
key_cases.quote: subsection C requires the court to determine whether the parent has been unwilling or unable to remedy the problems during the period in which he has been offered rehabilitation services
